title: At the restaurant
goal: Read a menu, order a full meal, and say which option you like better.
bekal: express degrees of liking (*gern – lieber – am liebsten*)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ein Abendessen zu zweit
dialogs.intro: Budi and Lena are having dinner at a German restaurant. German menus are full of long compound words — and almost all of them break down into two short words you already know.

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.id: Good evening. Do you have a reservation?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Nein, aber ist ein Tisch für zwei frei?
lines.id: No, but is there a table for two free?
lines.literal: no, but is a table for two free?

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.text: Ja, dort am Fenster. Hier ist die Speisekarte.
lines.id: Yes, over there by the window. Here's the menu.
lines.literal: yes, there at-the window. here is the food-card.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you. What do you recommend?

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.text: Das Schnitzel ist heute sehr gut. Und die Gemüsesuppe als Vorspeise.
lines.id: The schnitzel is very good today. And the vegetable soup as a starter.
lines.literal: the schnitzel is today very good. and the vegetable-soup as starter.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Ich esse gern Fisch. Haben Sie auch Fisch?
lines.id: I like fish. Do you have fish too?
lines.literal: I eat gladly fish. have you also fish?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Perfekt, das nehme ich. Und als Getränk ein Glas Weißwein.
lines.id: Perfect, I'll have that. And to drink, a glass of white wine.
lines.literal: perfect, that take I. and as drink a glass white-wine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich esse lieber Fleisch. Ich nehme das Schnitzel mit Pommes.
lines.id: I prefer meat. I'll have the schnitzel with fries.
lines.literal: I eat rather meat. I take the schnitzel with fries.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ein großes Bier, bitte. Kein Alkohol für mich — ein alkoholfreies.
lines.id: A large beer, please. No alcohol for me — an alcohol-free one.
lines.literal: a large beer, please. no alcohol for me — an alcohol-free.

lines.speaker: Kellner:
lines.id: Very good. Enjoy your meal later!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sehr gut, danke! Besser als in Berlin.
lines.id: Very good, thanks! Better than in Berlin.
lines.literal: very good, thanks! better than in Berlin.

notes: **Long compound words are just stacks of short ones.** *Speisekarte* = *Speise* (dish) + *Karte* (card). *Gemüsesuppe* = *Gemüse* + *Suppe*. The gender always comes from the **last word**: *die Karte* → *die Speisekarte*, *die Suppe* → *die Gemüsesuppe*. This rule works for words of any length.

***gern → lieber → am liebsten*.** Three levels of liking: *Ich esse **gern** Fisch* (like), *Ich esse **lieber** Fleisch* (prefer), *Ich esse **am liebsten** Pizza* (like best). This is the most common way to state a preference, and it's completely irregular — learn the three together.

***schmecken*** is used specifically for how food tastes: *Wie schmeckt es?* ("how does it taste?"), *Es schmeckt gut* ("it's good"). German doesn't use *gut sein* for taste — *Das Essen ist gut* sounds like rating the quality, not the flavor.
***Guten Appetit!*** is said before eating, and the reply is simply *Danke, gleichfalls* ("thanks, you too"). At a table with Germans, nobody starts eating before this has been said.
**Line 9: *Ich esse lieber Fleisch*.** Notice where *lieber* goes — right after the verb, just like *gern*. Both are adverbs, not verbs, so neither ever stands alone as an answer.

***als*** in the last line means "than" and is used for comparing: *besser als*, *größer als*, *teurer als*. It's the same *als* you saw in unit 6 meaning "as" — once again, its position decides its meaning.

grammars.title: Expressing likes: three levels
body: German has two ways of saying you like something. The first puts *gern* after the verb — used for **activities**. The second uses *mögen* — used for **things**.
after: ⚠️ Look at the last column of row four: *mögen* is negated with ***kein***, not *nicht*, because what's being negated is the noun. *Ich mag **keinen** Fisch*, *Ich mag **keine** Milch*.

*Mögen* and *möchten* are related but not interchangeable: *Ich **mag** Kaffee* = I like coffee (in general); *Ich **möchte** einen Kaffee* = I'd like a coffee (now, here). Ordering with *Ich mag einen Kaffee* sounds strange.

grammars.title: Comparing things
body: Comparisons are made by adding **-er** to the adjective, and the comparing word is **als** — just like English "cheap**er** than". Short adjectives with a, o, u usually take an Umlaut as well.

head: Adjective
More…
Most…
Example
rows: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.

after: The last three rows are completely irregular, and they're the ones used most. The good news: there are only three — just like English *good – better – best*.
To say **the same**, use *so … wie*: *Berlin ist **so** teuer **wie** München.* Notice the comparing word changes from *als* to *wie* — using *als* here is a mistake even some native speakers make.
At A1 you only need these forms **after the verb** (*Das ist billiger*). Using them in front of a noun (*ein billigeres Hotel*) requires adjective endings, which come apart in A2.

blocks.text: German menus almost always follow the same order. Recognizing the four section headings is enough to know where to look.

⚠️ If you don't eat pork, the sentence to memorize is ***Ich esse kein Schweinefleisch***, plus the question ***Ist da Schweinefleisch drin?*** ("is there pork in it?"). Pork is very common in German cooking, including in sausages and soups whose names don't mention it. For vegetarians: *Ich bin Vegetarier / Vegetarierin*, and *Haben Sie etwas Vegetarisches?*

head: German
English
rows: Haben Sie einen Tisch für zwei?
Do you have a table for two?
Als Vorspeise nehme ich die Suppe.
As a starter I'll have the soup.

blocks.title: When something's wrong
items: *Entschuldigung, das habe ich nicht bestellt.* — Excuse me, I didn't order this.
*Die Suppe ist kalt.* — The soup is cold.
*Können wir bitte noch Wasser haben?* — Could we have some more water, please?
*Ich glaube, die Rechnung stimmt nicht.* — I think the bill isn't right.

blocks.text: All the complaints above open with *Entschuldigung* and end on a questioning note, not an accusing one. That works far better than a blunt statement — which, without any softening words, easily sounds rude in German.

items: Haben Sie einen Tisch für zwei?
Ich esse ____ Pizza — das ist mein Lieblingsessen. (like best)
Fährst du ____ mit dem Bus oder mit dem Rad? (prefer)

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: für zwei / haben Sie / einen Tisch
als / besser / in Berlin / das schmeckt
